video_title: I Was the Algorithm Before Algorithms Then I Had to Start Over · Scott Pulcini
gist: Former E-mini S&P mega-scalper Scott Pulcini (about 10% of volume, $10M in 2003) explains how algos, the end of legal spoofing and the CME pulling counterparty data destroyed his order-book edge, and how he rebuilt with CME MBO iceberg/stop-run data on Bookmap plus Spot Gamma options flow and GEX levels. He stresses volume and volatility (ATR) based sizing, hard loss limits (after two $800K tilt days) and rules-based trading in a headline-driven market.

themes.theme: Edge decay: from floor-era scalping to algos

insights.claim: In the early-2000s electronic futures market, NASDAQ futures bid/ask quotes were sometimes 100 points apart and still got filled on both sides, an edge so wide that marginal traders made money.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Shows how quickly microstructure edges get competed away once electronic markets mature; extreme spreads are a transient regime.
insights.quote: literally a monkey could have done it

insights.claim: Scott Pulcini scalped roughly 10% of E-mini S&P volume (about 50,000 contracts round-trip per day) and made about $10 million in 2003, trading up to 3,000 contracts at a time.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin)
insights.so_what: Benchmark for how much size a discretionary order-book scalper could carry before algos dominated.

insights.claim: Large-size scalping was viable pre-2007 because displayed order-book size was real (thousand-lots were genuine), so a scalper could buy 1,000 and exit against 2,000-3,000 lots resting below with little risk.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Explains why depth-of-market reading lost its value once displayed liquidity became unreliable.
insights.quote: if you saw a thousand lot in the order book it was a thousand lot

insights.claim: Spoofing (placing size with no intention to trade to push the market) was legal until roughly 2007-2008, and Pulcini says he routinely stacked the book to scare price in his direction.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Regulatory change removed a core tool of floor-era scalpers; regulation is a key driver of microstructure edge.

insights.claim: The CME once exposed counterparty house numbers, letting traders see whether they were trading against a known local or an unknown large house; Pulcini says the CME pulled that data under pressure from its biggest commission-paying firms, starting the erosion of his edge.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Exchange data-policy decisions can create or destroy entire trading edges overnight; watch exchange data products.
insights.quote: They make money by commission. They're going to listen to whoever their biggest commission players are.

insights.claim: Today E-mini S&P displayed depth is mostly 20-50 lots instead of thousands, and large visible orders are usually pulled as price approaches, so algos run most markets most of the time.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Visible depth is not tradable information; liquidity is fleeting and algorithmic.
insights.quote: these algos just are running the show in most of these markets most of the time

insights.claim: Pulcini says reading the depth-of-market order book no longer offers a consistent edge for humans because orders are constantly put in and pulled and no human is faster than a computer.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Retail 'DOM reading' education is selling an obsolete edge; rely on order-type data instead.
insights.quote: There's no edge anymore in that a consistent edge.

insights.claim: Pulcini was knocked out of trading by around 2013 through a combination of low volatility, rising algorithmic trading and a manipulative rival, spent about seven years in medical sales, and returned only after Dr. Brett Steamberger showed him Bookmap.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Even top-decile traders' edges are regime-dependent; career/strategy durability requires adaptation.

insights.claim: The core lesson of edge decay is that the best edge can stop working suddenly, and traders must find a new expression of their strengths rather than wait for the old market to return.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: For any strategy (or fund relying on one), plan for edge obsolescence rather than mean reversion of conditions.
insights.quote: you can have the best edge in the world and think you've made it and all of a sudden the rug's pulled and it doesn't work anymore

insights.claim: A large rival local known by house number 990 could put on 6,000 contracts and allegedly manipulated E-mini S&P by crossing his own orders to fake large buying, luring traders to chase into his offers, then pulling everything.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Wash-trade-style manipulation historically targeted thin, lunchtime liquidity; similar patterns now run via algos.
insights.quote: he was crossing his own borders which is the most illegal thing you can do in the market

insights.claim: The manipulation clustered around 10:15 and 12:30 Central when New York and Chicago institutional traders were at lunch, and Pulcini still advises avoiding trading at those times.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Midday low-liquidity windows are more prone to engineered moves; reduce size or stand aside then.
insights.quote: Do not trade at that time of day if you can avoid it.

insights.claim: Pulcini says regulatory penalties for market manipulation are trivial relative to profits, comparing the rival's eventual ~2016 futures ban and fine to biotech firms paying $10 million fines on billion-dollar gains.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Enforcement is not a reliable deterrent; assume manipulation persists as a cost of doing business.

insights.claim: Pulcini believes someone often trades ahead of scheduled data releases, citing 4,000-lot E-mini S&P buy icebergs appearing 30 seconds before a 9 o'clock number.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Pre-release order flow can leak information; watch for anomalous large orders just before macro prints.
insights.quote: All of a sudden 4,000 bias comes in the E- mini S&P 30 seconds before the number.

insights.claim: Pulcini claims people are paying about $100,000 a month for early access to Trump's social media posts seconds before the public, illustrating how headline trading is gamed.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Headline-driven moves may be front-run by paid early access; retail is structurally late to political headlines.

insights.claim: Algos front-run displayed large orders by placing offers above and pushing price to make the big entity chase, which is why institutions hide size in iceberg orders.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Explains the prevalence of hidden/iceberg liquidity and why displayed size is misleading.
insights.quote: these ALOS will frontr run that order trying to make that that big entity chase

themes.theme: CME MBO data: icebergs and stop runs

insights.claim: Pulcini calls the CME's enhanced market-by-order (MBO) data, which identifies iceberg orders and stop runs by order ID, the most powerful and durable edge he has seen, trading it for about nine years.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Order-type-level exchange data is a premium data product; demand for it supports CME data revenue and platforms like Bookmap.
insights.quote: the most powerful thing I've ever seen as far as an edge in the markets

insights.claim: Because MBO data carries order IDs and order types, it distinguishes stop runs from iceberg orders with certainty, unlike educators who infer stop runs from new highs.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Precise order-type data removes guesswork about whether a move was stops or institutional size.

insights.claim: Stop runs usually reflect retail traders 'puking' rather than initiative buying, so a buy-stop run into a level you already wanted to short is a higher-probability reversal signal.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Use forced-liquidation flow as contrarian confirmation at pre-identified levels.
insights.quote: That big big green candle was a was just a puke, guys.

insights.claim: Big-money sell iceberg orders are right more often than not, and repeated icebergs at a level eventually move the market, but they are not right every time.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Track where institutions hide size; it skews probabilities, not certainties.
insights.quote: the big money is not right all the time

insights.claim: Pulcini validates iceberg/stop events by waiting for price to push one 5-minute ATR out of the zone; if it can fight the algos that far, continuation probability rises sharply.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: A volatility-normalized breakout filter for order-flow signals.

insights.claim: Pulcini only trades iceberg events above market-specific size thresholds: at least 700 contracts in the E-mini S&P and 150 in NASDAQ futures.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Signals must be scaled to each market's liquidity to be tradable.

insights.claim: Pulcini scans crude, gold, Russell, Dow, E-mini S&P, NASDAQ, soybeans and wheat for iceberg/stop events, using cross-market coverage instead of fast manual order-book processing.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Event-driven signals scale across markets; breadth replaces speed as the human edge.

themes.theme: Options flow and gamma as market driver

insights.claim: Pulcini says real-time options flow (Spot Gamma's HIRO, hedging impact of real-time options) is now close to or tied with iceberg data as the top driver of futures, with options dealers' hedging driving futures rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Options-driven dealer hedging is the tail wagging the dog; monitor options flow to anticipate futures moves.
insights.quote: It's not the futures driving the options. It's it's the options driving the futures

insights.claim: When entities buy puts or sell calls, non-directional dealers on the other side must hedge in futures or the underlying stock, mechanically pushing price; Pulcini calls this the newest form of manipulation.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Large options trades transmit directly into futures/stock price via hedging; useful for intraday timing.

insights.claim: Pulcini estimates that algos (like price-change mean-reversion algos) plus options flow account for about 95% of daily trading, with only about 5% being genuine program buying or selling by big funds, which shows up as heavy relative volume.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Most intraday moves are noise/mechanical; real institutional flow is rare and identifiable via relative volume.

insights.claim: Gamma exposure (GEX) levels, including zero-days-to-expiration levels, act as magnets and then support/resistance because dealers hedge there; a buy iceberg at a GEX level is one of Pulcini's highest-conviction auto-entry setups.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Confluence of dealer gamma levels and institutional order flow is a high-probability level.
insights.quote: they're like magnets

insights.claim: Pulcini argues the two biggest market drivers are volume and volatility, and any level or indicator only matters if confirmed by volume.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Filter technical levels through volume/volatility rather than adding indicators.
insights.quote: the the two biggest things that drive markets are volume and volatility

insights.claim: Static stops (e.g., risking 20 NASDAQ points to make 60) fail when the 5-minute ATR jumps to 90 points, as happened often over the past year of news-driven trading, so stops and size must scale to ATR.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Volatility-adjusted sizing is essential in headline-heavy regimes.

insights.claim: When relative volume (compared with the same time window over the prior 30 days) is under 100%, Pulcini expects choppy, whipsaw trade where price-change algos snap back moves that go too far too fast.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Low relative volume favors mean-reversion over breakout trades.

insights.claim: Pulcini risks about $500 per strategy and caps daily losses at about 5-6% of the account, with 1-2% risk per trade, enforced by a firm-level shutoff.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Concrete risk parameters for discretionary futures trading.

insights.claim: Pulcini sizes 2-4x normal only on A+ setups where the real-time volume event matches a thesis built from balance areas, a practice he learned at SMB Capital where traders who fail to size up on A+ setups are sent to the simulator.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Asymmetric sizing on highest-conviction setups drives returns; consistency otherwise.
insights.quote: you've got to go for the throat

insights.claim: Markets are either trending or balancing; breakouts from balance occur because traders positioned wrong in that area must exit, but balance areas differ by how much volume built them.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Volume-weighted balance areas indicate the fuel available for a breakout.

insights.claim: Pulcini lost about $800,000 in four minutes in February 2004 after his firm stopped enforcing his $100,000 daily loss limit, then repeated it a month later, costing $1.4 million he says a hard limit would have saved.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Hard, externally enforced loss limits are critical; discretionary overrides fail under tilt.
insights.quote: If I just were respected my loss limit I have an I would have an extra $1.4 million in my bank account.

insights.claim: Negative reinforcement, getting away with breaking a risk rule, makes traders repeat it until it causes a catastrophic loss.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Risk-limit exceptions are dangerous precisely because they often work initially.

insights.claim: Pulcini says his gut feel, once his main edge, is now wrong about 80% of the time because algos are designed to do the opposite of how traders think, so he trades strictly rules-based 'like an algo'.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Discretionary intuition has degraded as an edge in algo-dominated markets.
insights.quote: I'm wrong 80% of the time

insights.claim: The smartest traders (physicists, doctors, lawyers) tend to struggle because they need a reason for every market move and keep adding indicators; simpler setups perform better.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Complexity is not edge; beware over-engineered strategies.

insights.claim: Turning off the live P&L display helped Pulcini scale up, because thinking of trades in real-world money terms causes panicky exits; size felt the same to him at 1 lot or 1,000 lots.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Detaching from P&L is a prerequisite for scaling size.

insights.claim: Pulcini calls the last year and a half the most difficult period of his 25 years due to tariff headlines and Trump-Iran headline 'ping pong', saying breakeven futures traders over that span are doing well.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Headline-driven regimes punish intraday futures strategies; expect wider stops and lower returns.
insights.quote: if you're just even breaking even the last year and a half trading futures, you're you're doing pretty well

insights.claim: Traders who depend on trading income to support their family almost never succeed, Pulcini estimates maybe one in a thousand, because needing to win distorts decisions.
insights.speaker: Scott Pulcini
insights.so_what: Have a separate income source before relying on trading returns.
